subtype: Approach: structured job search with weekly targets [Action]
passage:
Monday. Trisha wrote a weekly plan on a card: refresh the CV, send ten applications, write to five old teammates, and rehearse one mock interview. Karthik agreed to be the interviewer on Friday.

Thursday. Six applications were in and three colleagues had been messaged. No replies yet. Trisha ticked the boxes anyway, because the ticks were the progress.

Friday. The mock interview with Karthik went badly on the first answer and better on the second. Karthik pointed to two weak spots. The week ended with a new card and a slightly different list. Trisha said the plan did not make the replies come faster, but it made each day feel less empty.

qa.q: How many applications did the weekly plan say to send?
qa.a: The weekly plan said to send ten applications.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel about the ticks on the card?
qa.a: Trisha felt that the ticks were progress, so each day felt less empty even without replies.

qa.q: What could Trisha add if replies stay slow, and why?
qa.a: Trisha could ask a former colleague to review the CV, because fresh eyes may find what stops replies.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the part played in the mock interview?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels helpful, because pointing to two weak spots gave Trisha a clear thing to fix.

grounding: An employee makes a weekly plan of updating the CV, applying, messaging former colleagues and practising, which gives a sense of progress when replies are slow.

subtype: Approach: structured job search with weekly targets [Action]
passage:
Farhan, you've been refreshing that job site all morning. Sit down. When I was twenty-two, and yes, I'm talking about Suraj, the old man at the corner desk, my first company shut in a week.
For a month I did what you're doing. Refresh, sigh, sleep late. Nothing happened.
Then my neighbour, a retired schoolteacher, made me write a weekly plan on the back of a calendar. Monday: fix one part of the CV. By Wednesday: ten applications, properly read, not blind clicks. By Friday: message five people I'd worked with. Saturday: one mock interview with a friend.
Replies were slow. Some weeks, none. But every Saturday I could tick the boxes, and that kept me sane. In the seventh week, one of those five messages turned into an interview. That's how I got here.
So. Take a calendar, Farhan. Monday, CV. Go.

qa.q: How many applications did young Suraj aim for by Wednesday?
How did young Suraj feel ticking the boxes on Saturdays?
qa.a: Steadier and more hopeful; the routine kept despair away even when replies were slow.

qa.q: Which part of the plan in the story turned into the job, and why might that be?
qa.a: Messaging five former colleagues each week; people who knew Suraj's work could vouch for it in a way applications alone could not.

qa.q: What might the retired schoolteacher have seen in young Suraj?
qa.a: Someone stuck and drifting who needed structure more than a lecture, which is why a weekly plan came first.

grounding: Shows a laid-off employee following weekly targets for CV updates, applications, messages to former colleagues and a mock interview.

subtype: Approach: structured job search with weekly targets [Action]
passage:
Hemant's laptop had belonged to the company, so when the layoff came, it went too. That left his phone, with a cracked screen, and the district library in Bhopal, open ten to five, with four computers and a queue.
He made a plan anyway and pinned it inside his wallet. Each week: fix one section of the CV on Monday. Ten applications by Thursday, two a day in the library slots. Five messages to former colleagues from his phone at night. One mock interview on Saturday with Usha, his old team lead, who had offered.
The first week he managed seven applications; the library's power went off twice. He moved the missing three to Friday morning, arriving at 9:45 to be first in line.
By the fourth week there had been two replies and one rejection. Not much. But every Saturday he could tell Usha exactly what he had done, and he stopped lying awake doing sums in the dark.

qa.q: When is the district library open?
What does Hemant arriving at 9:45 suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He is determined not to let the missing applications slide, and the routine is making him feel more in control.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do about not having a laptop?
qa.a: Ask Usha or former colleagues whether anyone has an old laptop to lend, or book a cyber café slot on busy days.

qa.q: What is Saturday like for Usha?
qa.a: Usha gets a clear account of Hemant's week to practise with, which makes it easier to help and to see progress.

grounding: Shows a laid-off employee keeping weekly targets for CV work, applications, messages and a mock interview despite having no laptop.
